Editor’s note
:
Corrigendum released
August 26, 2009. Original judgment has been
corrected with text of corrigendum appended.

IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Bank of Montreal v. Tortora,

2009 BCSC 1140

Date: 20090821

Docket:
S090068

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Bank of Montreal

Plaintiff

And

Giuseppina Tortora also known as
Josephine

Tortora, Shenaz Poonja and Shaffin Punja

also known as Shaffin Poonja

Defendants

Corrected
Judgment:  The text of the judgment has been corrected

at paragraph 54 where a change was made on August 26, 2009

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Butler

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

J. Geoffrey Howard

Joanne Kuroyama

Counsel for the
Defendant, Giuseppina Tortora also known as Josephine Tortora:

David G. Perry

Steven W. Lesiuk

Counsel for
the Defendants, Shenaz Poonja and Shaffin Punja also known as Shaffin Poonja:

Nazeer T. Mitha

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

July 22, 23 and 24, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

August 21, 2009

[
1
]

The Bank of Montreal (the “Bank”) has brought
this action against Giuseppina Tortora and Shenaz Poonja, two former employees,
alleging breaches of their employment contracts, gross negligence, breach of
their fiduciary duties, constructive fraud, conspiracy, and unjust enrichment.
In addition, the Bank advances claims against Shaffin Punja, Ms. Poonja’s
husband, in conspiracy and unjust enrichment.

[
2
]

As the case management judge, I heard
applications brought by the defendants during the course of a three-day hearing
in July 2009.  I issued rulings on many of the applications and indicated that
I would deliver brief written reasons for those rulings.  I also said that I
would deliver my rulings on additional applications at the same time.  These
are my reasons for the rulings on the various applications under Rule 19(24)
and Rule 24 of the
Rules of Court
,
B.C. Reg. 221/90
[the
Rules
of Court
].

Background

[
3
]

Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja were both long-time
employees of the Bank.  Ms. Tortora was a Mortgage Specialist who received a
salary plus commissions for mortgages that she brought to the Bank.  Ms. Poonja
was a Financial Services Manager who processed mortgage applications, including
some of those from Ms. Tortora.  The Bank terminated both Ms. Tortora and Ms.
Poonja from their positions in December 2008, shortly before this action was
commenced.

[
4
]

The claims arise out of two principle
allegations.  First, the Bank alleges that Ms. Tortora secretly split
commissions she earned with Ms. Poonja by providing funds to Mr. Punja.  Ms.
Poonja was not entitled to receive commissions under her employment contract.  The
Bank alleges that splitting commissions is contrary to the Bank’s code of
business conduct and ethics (the “Code”) and its policies, standards,
subsidiary policies, and operating directives (the “Policies”).  It further
alleges that the breaches of the Bank's Code and Policies by Ms. Tortora and
Ms. Poonja amount to breaches of their employment contracts and breaches of
their fiduciary duties owed to the Bank.  The Bank further alleges that all
three defendants conspired to secretly split the commissions.

[
5
]

The Bank’s second allegation is that Ms. Tortora
and Ms. Poonja were grossly negligent in arranging and approving ten mortgages
in Ontario (the “Papas Mortgages”).  The Bank alleges that both Ms. Tortora and
Ms. Poonja breached the Bank's Code and Policies in relation to the Papas
Mortgages in various ways, including through the acceptance of appraisals that
had been fraudulently altered.  The Bank makes no allegations against Mr. Punja
in relation to the Papas Mortgages.

[
6
]

The statement of claim in this matter was issued
on January 6, 2009.  After the defendants raised issues regarding the lack of
particulars and other inadequacies in the statement of claim, the Bank filed an
amended statement of claim on March 4, 2009.  The original statement of claim,
which was approximately 14 pages in length, was completely crossed out and
replaced by a new 34-page statement of claim.

[
7
]

The defendants issued a notice of motion seeking
to dismiss the Bank’s claims pursuant to Rule 18 of the
Rules of Court
.
At the same time, they applied to strike certain allegations in the statement
of claim pursuant to Rule 19(24).  At a case management conference, I directed
that the Rule 19 applications be heard prior to the summary judgment
application.  Accordingly, I heard those applications along with an application
pursuant to Rule 24.

Rulings
of July 24, 2009 – Applications Pursuant to Rule 19(24) and Rule 24

[
8
]

The defendants applied to strike the Bank’s
claims based on breaches of fiduciary duty, breaches of contract, negligence,
constructive fraud and unjust enrichment.  The applications were based on
subrules 19(24)(a) to (d).  I dismissed these applications for reasons that can
be stated briefly.

[
9
]

Rule 19(24) provides:

(24)      At any stage of a proceeding the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an
endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)  it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b)  it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)  it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d)  it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
10
]

The applications were based, principally, on subrule
(a);  the defendants argued that the statement of claim disclosed no reasonable
claim.  There is no issue as to the proper approach on these applications.  The
Court proceeds on the assumption that all facts pleaded are true:
McNaughton
v. Baker
,
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, [1988] 4 W.W.R. 742 at 748; 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (S.C.).  The
applicant must establish that it is “plain and obvious” that the pleading
discloses no reasonable cause of action:
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,

1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at 972, 74 D.L.R. (4th) 321.  The mere fact that a case is
weak, not likely to proceed, or novel is no ground for striking the pleading:
Minnes
v. Minnes
(1962),
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39 W.W.R. 112 at 112, 34 D.L.R. (2d) 497 (C.A.).

[
11
]

With regard to subrules (b) and (c), the tests
are similar.  The applicant must show it is “plain and obvious” or “beyond a
reasonable doubt” that the action is certain to fail.  In other words, the
applicant must demonstrate that it is clear the allegations in the statement of
claim are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or would prejudice,
embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding:
347202
B.C. Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 449
(S.C.)
, and
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish
Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (S.C.) [
Citizens
].  In

Citizens
, Romilly J. nicely summarized the law relating to
subrules (b) and (c) at para. 47:

Irrelevancy and
embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it is
difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.). An
"embarrassing" and "scandalous" pleading is one that is so
irrelevant that it will involve the parties in useless expense and will
prejudice the trial of the action by involving them in a dispute apart from the
issues:
Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147
(B.C.C.A.). An allegation which is scandalous will not be struck if it is
relevant to the proceedings. It will only be struck if irrelevant as well as
scandalous:
College of Dental Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66
W.W.R. 499 (B.C.C.A.). A pleading is "unnecessary" or
"vexatious" if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff's cause
of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan
,

1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.). A pleading that is superfluous will not
be struck out if it is not necessarily unnecessary or otherwise objectionable:
Lutz
v. Canadian Puget Sound Lumber and Timber Co.

(1920), 28 B.C.R 39 (C.A.)
. A
pleading is "frivolous" if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the
sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of
estoppel:
Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.
(July 13, 1992), Doc.
Prince George Registry 20714 (B.C. Master).

Breach
of Fiduciary Duty

[
12
]

The defendants argue that the relationship
between the Bank and its two former employees does not come within any recognized
category of fiduciary relationship.  They say that the Bank has failed to
allege in the pleadings the three general characteristics of a fiduciary
relationship:

a)         scope
for the exercise of discretion or power;

b)         the unilateral ability to exercise discretion or power so
as to affect the beneficiary’s interests; and

c)         the peculiar vulnerability of the beneficiary to the
exercise of the discretion or power by the fiduciary.

[
13
]

The defendants further say that, taken as a
whole, the pleadings indicate that the two former employees had little or no
ability to exercise discretion.  This argument is based on the detailed
pleadings regarding the Bank’s Policies and Code, which the Bank says Ms.
Tortora and Ms. Poonja were required to follow.  They also argue that it would
be extremely unusual for an employee who is not at a senior management or
directorship level to be a fiduciary.

[
14
]

The Bank’s allegations in the amended statement
of claim in relation to Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja are very similar.  In
paragraph 17 of the amended statement of claim, the Bank alleges the following
against Ms. Tortora:

Tortora held a
position whereby she had the power to control the information and flow of
information upon which loan decisions were made and was in a position of
special relationship with the Bank for the reasons set out in paragraph 15.  The
Bank was vulnerable to the exercise of power or control over its mortgage
lending function by this former employee, who was, in the carrying out of her
duties, able to impact and prejudice the legal position or practical business
position of the Bank by failing to comply with the Code and Policies.  Therefore,
Tortora owed the bank a fiduciary duty which included a duty to avoid conflicts
of duty and self interest.

[
15
]

The allegations, which I must assume are true,
do set forth the necessary averments for a claim based on breach of fiduciary
duty.  The fact that the claim may seem incongruous or novel given the status
of employment of the two defendants is no reason to strike the claim pursuant
to Rule 19(24)(a).  While it is rare for an employee of less than senior
management or directorial status to be subject to a fiduciary duty, there is no
doubt that, in certain circumstances, such a finding is possible:
Barton
Insurance Brokers Ltd. v. Irwin
,
1999 BCCA 73
at para.
40
, 170 D.L.R.
(4th) 69, and
South Nahanni Trading Co. v. Gravel
(2007),
2007 CanLII 30668 (ON SC)
, 36
C.B.R. (5th) 115 (Ont. Sup. Ct.).  It is not plain and obvious that a claim for
breach of fiduciary duty is bound to fail.

Breach
of Contract

[
16
]

Ms. Tortora argues that the claims in contract
offend subrules (b) to (d) of Rule 19(24).  She says that the allegations are
difficult to follow as they are spread throughout the lengthy statement of
claim and are not separated from the pleadings of other causes of action.  She
relies on
Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia
(1998),
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, 25
C.P.C. (4th) 107 (B.C.S.C.) [
Homalco
] to argue that the pleadings
should be struck because they are prolix and convoluted and are, thus,
embarrassing.

[
17
]

In
Homalco
at para.
11
, K. Smith
J. found that the statement of claim was an embarrassing pleading because it
contained much that was unnecessary and was constructed in a manner calculated
to confuse.  He found it to be difficult to respond to and, thus, prejudicial.
He struck the entire statement of claim, but granted leave to amend.

[
18
]

Here, there is some merit in the argument that
the claims based on breach of contract are not drafted in what K. Smith J.
described at para. 9 of
Homalco
as “the traditional way”.  The
pleading does not allege that particular provisions set out in a written
employment contract were breached by the defendants.  However, the gist of the
breach of contract claims is clear upon reading the entire document.  The Bank
says that the defendants failed to follow the Bank’s Policies and Code.  The
particular Policies and Code are set out in some detail.  The Bank alleges that
the failure to do so amounts to a breach of the employment contract by both Ms.
Tortora and Ms. Poonja.  The Bank asserts that both of these defendants
acknowledged in writing their awareness of and compliance with the Bank’s Code
on specific dates.  It also alleges breaches of an implied term of the
employment contracts with these defendants.  The implied term is alleged to
arise pursuant to the common law:  an obligation to carry out duties with
honesty, fidelity, and good faith.

[
19
]

The fact that claims may be novel or have
possible weaknesses does not make them embarrassing or prejudicial.  The basis
of the claims in contract can be easily discerned from the pleading.  Those
portions of the statement of claim that the defendants say are irrelevant may
well be relevant once evidence is presented regarding the employment
relationships.  The defendants will not have difficulty responding to the
statement of claim.  There is no reason to strike the contract claims.  It is
not plain and obvious that the allegations are embarrassing, prejudicial, or
unnecessary.

Negligence

[
20
]

The defendants argue that it is unclear if the
statement of claim is alleging both negligence and gross negligence against Ms.
Tortora and Ms. Poonja.  With regard to the claims in gross negligence, they
say that the statement of claim fails to set out material facts to assert the
standard of care, the breaches of that standard, and damages.

[
21
]

I do not accept the defendants’ arguments.  It
is clear that the claims advanced in negligence are based on allegations of
gross negligence.  Under the heading “Duty of Care”, the Bank has set out the
standard of care for both Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja.  The breaches of that
standard are based on the allegations that Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja failed to
follow policies and procedures in relation to the Papas Mortgages, which are
set out in some detail at paragraphs 76 to 89 of the amended statement of
claim.  The Bank has asserted that the breaches amount to gross negligence.  At
paragraph 93 of the amended statement of claim, the Bank asserts that the acts
and omissions of these two defendants amount to “a complete and utter failure
to carry out their duties and responsibilities as a Mortgage Specialist and a
Financial Service Manager, respectively”.

[
22
]

It is not plain and obvious that the pleading
discloses no cause of action in gross negligence.

Constructive
Fraud

[
23
]

The allegations in constructive fraud are made
in relation to the Papas Mortgages.  The Bank alleges that the assistance
provided by Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja to the mortgage broker who referred the
mortgages to the Bank and who fraudulently altered the appraisals, combined
with the defendants’ complete disregard for the Bank’s Policies and Code,
amounted to a constructive fraud and a breach of their fiduciary duties.

[
24
]

The defendants argue that constructive fraud is
not a cause of action.  Alternatively, they say that, if it is, it can only
arise where there is a breach of a fiduciary duty.

[
25
]

As I have already found, the amended statement
of claim does disclose a breach of fiduciary duty claim.  Hence, the
alternative argument cannot succeed.  I also find that the amended statement of
claim alleges the kind of breach of obligation that might give rise to a
constructive fraud claim.  In other words, it alleges conduct falling below the
standards demanded by equity:  wilful blindness and recklessness in
circumstances where the other party (here, the Bank) is vulnerable because of
the nature of the relationship.  As the Bank argued, a claim in constructive
fraud has long been recognized as arising in circumstances where the actions of
the defendants do not involve deceit or actual fraud:
Nocton v.
Ashburton
,
[1914] A.C. 932 (H.L.)
.  While such a claim is similar to
and may be co-extensive with a claim in breach of fiduciary duty, it is not
plain and obvious that the claim discloses no reasonable cause of action.

Unjust
Enrichment

[
26
]

The Bank alleges that Ms. Tortora was unjustly
enriched by commissions that she received from the Papas Mortgages.  It also
alleges that Ms. Poonja and Mr. Punja were unjustly enriched when they “in
turn” received funds from Ms. Tortora with respect to the Papas Mortgages.  The
Bank alleges that it was deprived with regard to those commissions and that
there was no juristic reason for that deprivation.

[
27
]

The defendants rely on
Isaac v. Guardian
Capital Group Limited
,
2004 BCSC 254
for the proposition that unjust
enrichment can only exist where there is no contract on which to base the
claim.  Here, they say that Ms. Tortora’s employment contract permitted payment
of commissions to her so there can be no unjust enrichment claim against her.
In the case of Ms. Poonja, the defendants say that it is unclear how the unjust
enrichment occurred;  there is nothing that specifies what payments were made
“in turn” from Ms. Tortora to Ms. Poonja.  Further, as the payments to Ms.
Poonja came from Ms. Tortora, there can be no deprivation of the Bank
corresponding to any enrichment she received.  Even if the allegation intends
to refer to commission splitting, the defendants say that the Bank suffered no
deprivation because there was a juristic reason – the employment contract – for
the payments to Ms. Tortora.

[
28
]

These arguments misstate the ruling of Melnick
J. in
Isaac
.  As Melnick J. noted at para. 38 of
Isaac
,
even though the plaintiff in that case advanced a claim based on a breach of
contract, the claim in unjust enrichment could be maintained as an alternative
claim.  He specifically permitted the plaintiff in that case to amend the
unjust enrichment claim to properly plead it.

[
29
]

Here, there is no question that the unjust
enrichment claims against Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja do plead the three
essential elements of the cause of action:

a)         the
defendants were enriched;

b)         the
Bank suffered a corresponding deprivation; and

c)         there
is no juristic reason for the deprivation.

[
30
]

When the amended statement of claim is read in
its entirety, it is also clear that the unjust enrichment claim against Ms.
Tortora is a claim made in the alternative to the principle allegation based on
breaches of her employment contract.  The deprivation of the Bank arising from
the payment to Ms. Tortora of commissions relating to the Papas Mortgages is clearly
pled.  There is no basis for striking the unjust enrichment claim against her.

[
31
]

The claim against Ms. Poonja is more
problematic.  However, when the amended statement of claim is read in its
entirety, it is evident that the unjust enrichment allegation against her is
also based on improper commission splitting.  It is, like the claim against Ms.
Tortora, an alternative claim to the principle allegation based on breaches of her
employment contract.  The deprivation the Bank alleges arises because it has
paid commissions that made their way to Ms. Poonja, who was not supposed to
receive them.  In this alternative claim, it is the breach of her fiduciary
obligations, rather than her employment contract, that gives rise to the
allegation that she was not to receive commissions.  While this claim is more
problematic than the claim based on contract, it is not plain and obvious that
no cause of action is disclosed by the amended pleading.

[
32
]

At the hearing in July 2009, I did not rule on
the unjust enrichment allegation against Mr. Punja.  The allegation against him
suffers from the same difficulty as the allegation against Ms. Poonja.  It is
not clear what funds he is said to have received, nor is it clear what
deprivation the Bank suffered.  Indeed, the only allegation is that payments were
made to him from Ms. Tortora.  No payments are alleged to have been made by the
Bank.  While the allegations contained in the whole of the amended statement of
claim do indicate deprivation suffered by the Bank for the payments allegedly
made by Ms. Tortora to Ms. Poonja, the same cannot be said for the payments
made “in turn” to Mr. Punja.  Mr. Punja has no relationship with the Bank that
would have caused the Bank to be deprived when he received funds from Ms.
Tortora.  Accordingly, the unjust enrichment allegation against Mr. Punja must
be struck.

Miscellaneous
Allegations

[
33
]

At the hearing in July 2009 there were two other
matters that I ordered struck from the amended statement of claim:

a)         the claim for aggravated damages in paragraph 113 and in
the prayer for relief; and

b)         the
reference to a claim for “wilful blindness” in the prayer for relief.

Application
Pursuant to Rule 24(3)

[
34
]

Ms. Poonja and Mr. Punja applied for an order
requiring the Bank to deliver an amended statement of claim that highlights
deletions and additions to the original statement of claim in a paragraph by
paragraph manner.  In other words, they argue that the amended statement of
claim does not satisfy Rule 24(3).  I dismissed this application.  No purpose
would be served by requiring the Bank to deliver its amended statement of claim
in this fashion.  The amended statement of claim, as delivered, does contain
the entire original document so it is possible to compare any section of the
amended statement of claim with the original to discern the changes or
additions.  The document proposed by Ms. Poonja and Mr. Punja would be more
difficult to read and less useful for the parties and the Court.  In any event,
the amended statement of claim, as prepared, does comply with Rule 24(3).

Conspiracy
Claim

[
35
]

At the hearing in July 2009, I did not rule on
the defendants’ application to strike the conspiracy claim.  That claim is
contained at paragraphs 98 to 106 of the amended statement of claim.  The Bank
alleges that Ms. Poonja was not entitled to receive any commissions under her
contract of employment.  It alleges that, in or before 2006, the three
defendants entered into a conspiracy to engage in the secret splitting of
commissions paid by the Bank to Ms. Tortora.  The Bank alleges that Ms. Tortora
made payments in excess of $245,000 to Mr. Punja and that he transferred funds
to his wife and paid for family expenses.  The Bank alleges that the Punja
family used the proceeds to fund an extravagant lifestyle.

[
36
]

At paragraphs 104 and 105 of the amended
statement of claim the Bank sets out the allegations of the unlawful conduct
used by the defendants to injure the Bank:

104.     It was an express term of the Code and an implied term of
their contracts of employment, that each of Tortora and Shenaz Poonja not take
unauthorized advantage of their employment in order to make a profit for
themselves and members of their family, which terms were breached and in respect
of which the Bank seeks to recover these improper payments.

105.     The splitting
of commissions between Tortora and her co-Defendants constituted a breach of
the Bank’s Code, a breach of the implied duty of fidelity, honesty and good
faith, a conspiracy, fraud and breach of fiduciary duty.

[
37
]

To establish a claim in conspiracy, the test set
out in
Canada Cement LaFarge Ltd. v. British Columbia Lightweight
Aggregate Ltd.
,
1983 CanLII 23 (SCC)
, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 452, [1983] 6 W.W.R. 385 [
Canada
Cement
], at 471-71 must be met:

Although the law
concerning the scope of the tort of conspiracy is far from clear, I am of the
opinion that whereas the law of tort does not permit an action against an
individual defendant who has caused injury to the plaintiff, the law of torts
does recognize a claim against them in combination as the tort of conspiracy
if:

(1)  whether the
means used by the defendants are lawful or unlawful, the predominant purpose of
the defendants' conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff; or,

(2)  where the
conduct of the defendants is unlawful, the conduct is directed towards the
plaintiff (alone or together with others), and the defendants should know in
the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result.

In situation
(2) it is not necessary that the predominant purpose of the defendants' conduct
be to cause injury to the plaintiff but, in the prevailing circumstances, it
must be a constructive intent derived from the fact that the defendants should
have known that injury to the plaintiff would ensue.  In both situations,
however, there must be actual damage suffered by the plaintiff.

[
38
]

The Bank makes no allegation in the amended
statement of claim that the predominant purpose of the defendants’ actions was
to injure the Bank.  The Bank is relying on the second branch of the conspiracy
test:  where the conduct of the defendants is unlawful.

[
39
]

The defendants argue that the statement of claim
does not disclose a cause of action in conspiracy because it does not allege
actual damages to the Bank.  They say that the only alleged damages are the
payments made by the Bank to Ms. Tortora as commissions.  Of course, the Bank
was obligated to make those payments pursuant to its employment contract with
her.  The only alleged damages are the splitting of commissions that should not
have been split.  The defendants say this does not amount to actual damages.
The defendants also argue that there is no pleading of any constructive intent
to injure the Bank.  In other words, the Bank has failed to allege that the commission
splitting was directed towards the Bank in circumstances where injury to the
Bank was likely to, and did, result.  With regard to the claims against Ms.
Tortora and Ms. Poonja, the defendants say that the conspiracy claim cannot
stand because it is merged with the claims in contract and breach of fiduciary
duty.

[
40
]

In addition, the defendants argue that there is
no allegation that Mr. Punja committed unlawful acts.  The defendants
acknowledge that the commission of a tort or breach of contract can amount to
an unlawful act for the purpose of a claim in civil conspiracy.  However, they
say that where the plaintiff relies upon the second branch of the conspiracy
test, all of the conspirators must have committed the allegedly unlawful acts.
Here, it is only Ms. Poonja and Ms. Tortora who are alleged to have breached
the Bank’s Code and Policies, their employment contracts, and their fiduciary
duties;  those are the only unlawful acts alleged against the conspirators.

[
41
]

In advancing this argument, the defendants rely
on
Normart Management Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co.
(1998),

1998 CanLII 2447 (ON CA)
, 155 D.L.R. (4th) 627, 37 O.R. (3d) 97 (C.A.), where the Court of Appeal struck
out conspiracy claims against officers and directors of the defendant companies
in circumstances where the defendant companies acquired certain properties to
the detriment of the plaintiff.  They also rely on the decision of Pitfield J.
in
Napoleone v. Baraldi
,
2004 BCSC 1065
, 48 B.L.R. (3d) 175, where
the plaintiff’s conspiracy claim against officers and directors of corporate
defendants was struck.  The claim against the corporate defendants in that case
was for wrongful dismissal.

[
42
]

The Bank opposes the application.  It says that
it has suffered actual damages as a result of the wrongful commission splitting.
It says that where employees have made unauthorized commissions or profit in
the course of their employment, courts usually award as damages the amount of
the unauthorized commission or profit:
Standard Life Assurance Co. v.
Horsburgh
,
2005 BCCA 108
, 46 B.C.L.R. (4th) 88.  In addition, the Bank
says that there are sufficient allegations in the pleading to allege a
constructive intent on the part of the defendants.

[
43
]

The Bank says that the defendants’ reliance on
Normart
Management
and
Napoleone
is misplaced.  It says those
cases can be distinguished because the plaintiffs in those cases were
attempting to lift the corporate veil and sue the officers and directors of the
defendant companies.  That is not the situation here.  The Bank also argues
that there is no need for it to allege that all of the conspirators committed
unlawful acts.  It says that the cause of action is made out where it is
alleged the conspirators agreed to a plan of action whereby one or some of them
carried out the unlawful conduct.  The Bank says it has alleged that Mr. Punja
was a party to the common design and relies on the following passage from
Clerk
& Lindsell on Torts
, 19th ed. (Toronto: Carswell, 2006) at 1613-14:

A person may be
a party to a combination to use unlawful means, even though he himself cannot
commit the unlawful acts in question, for example a person who joins parties to
a contract in threats that they will break that contract, thereby constituting
a conspiracy to intimidate. On the other hand, persons who participated in
meetings which formed part of the combination but who played no active role
will not be parties to the conspiracy.  The question is whether a particular
defendant, having regard to his knowledge, utterances and actions, was
sufficiently a party to the combination and the common design. [footnotes
omitted]

[
44
]

I have concluded that it is plain and obvious
that the amended statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action in
conspiracy against Mr. Punja.  I also conclude that there is no basis to permit
the conspiracy claim to continue against Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja because the
breaches of contract and fiduciary duty necessarily merge with the conspiracy
claim.

Conspiracy
Claim Against Mr. Punja

[
45
]

The key issue raised by this application is
whether, under the second branch of the conspiracy test, there must be an
allegation that each of the conspirators committed the unlawful acts.  In my
view, such an allegation is essential to a claim against a conspirator.  In
this case, the conspiracy claim against Mr. Punja cannot succeed because there
is no allegation that he committed a wrongful act.

[
46
]

Before the decision of the Supreme Court of
Canada in
Canada Cement
, Canadian courts wrestled with the
utility and wisdom of the tort of conspiracy.  The comments of Estey J. in that
case at 473 describe the tort as an anomaly:

The tort of
conspiracy to injure, even without the extension to include a conspiracy to
perform unlawful acts where there is a constructive intent to injure, has been
the target of much criticism throughout the common law world. It is indeed a
commercial anachronism as so aptly illustrated by Lord Diplock in
Lonrho
....
In fact, the action may have lost much of its usefulness in our commercial
world, and survives in our law as an anomaly.

[
47
]

The extension of the tort to include the second
branch of the conspiracy test was confirmed by that decision.  However, the
Court subsequently made it clear that the tort was not to be extended further.
In
Frame v. Smith
,
1987 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 99 at 109, 42 D.L.R. (4th) 81,
La Forest J. stated: “this Court has made it clear that it does not look kindly
upon the extension of this tort, which it regards as an anomaly”.

[
48
]

To extend a conspiracy claim to include co-conspirators
who are not alleged to have committed any wrongful conduct would be a further
extension of the tort.  It would be illogical if a claim in conspiracy could
succeed against someone who:

a)         did not have as his predominant purpose the intent to
cause injury to the plaintiff, and

b)         did not engage in any unlawful or wrongful conduct
directed towards the plaintiff.

Yet, if the Bank’s argument is accepted,
that is exactly the extension to the tort of conspiracy that would be created.
In essence it would create a third category of conspirator:  someone who does
not meet either of the first two branches of the test, but is drawn in because
of his familial or business relationship with another conspirator.

[
49
]

It is telling that the Bank was not able to refer
the Court to any case where a conspiracy claim was sustained in these
circumstances.  The comment in
Clerk & Lindsell
is of no assistance
to the Bank.  The reference for the statement at 1613 that “[a] person may be a
party to a combination to use unlawful means, even though he himself cannot
commit the unlawful acts in question” is
Rookes v. Barnard
,

[1964] A.C. 1129, [1964] 1 All E.R. 367 (H.L.)
.  That case is very different
from the case at bar.  In
Rookes
, the three defendant union
organizers each committed the tort of intimidation in attempting to get an
employer to fire an employee.  In other words, they did commit the unlawful act
in question.  In any event, the English law at that time did not recognize the
second branch of the tort of conspiracy, so the case is of no assistance to the
Bank.

[
50
]

Recently, in
Tracy (Representative ad
litem of) v. Instaloans Financial Solution Centres (B.C.) Ltd.
,
2009
BCCA 110
, 88 B.C.L.R. (4th) 201, our Court of Appeal was asked to consider
whether a conspiracy claim could be maintained against principals of companies
who conspired to have their companies commit unlawful acts to injure the
plaintiffs.  The defendants were companies that operated “payday loans” businesses;
the two individuals were officers and directors of the companies.  The
defendant companies made loans at rates of interest that exceeded those
permitted by
s. 347
of the
Criminal Code
, R.S.C. 1985, c.
C-46.  The action was certified as a class action and the chambers judge
decided a number of the common issues in a summary trial.  She found that the
companies and the two principals were liable in unjust enrichment and
conspiracy.

[
51
]

On appeal, the principals argued that they could
not be found liable in conspiracy for a number of reasons, including that the
criminal conduct was carried out by the companies, not the principals.  The court
specifically declined to decide that issue, but concluded as follows at paras. 28
and 29:

The fact the illegal activity was actually
conducted by the Instaloans companies would, in the circumstances, appear to be
of no consequence to the personal liability of Mr. Latimer and Mr. Arcand.  While
the primary reason individuals choose to incorporate is to protect themselves
from personal liability through the separate legal personality of the
corporation, as I have said, the law does not treat favourably individuals who
either incorporate a company for the purpose of undertaking a wrongful act, or
who, while acting as directors, cause the company to engage in a wrongful act.

However, this
said, the fact remains the Instaloans companies and their two principals are
jointly and severally liable for unjust enrichment such that it is not
necessary to actually decide whether, if it were otherwise, they would be
liable in tort.

[
52
]

As that issue was not decided, and the facts in
that case involved the commission of criminal acts by individuals attempting to
hide behind the corporate veil, I consider that I am not restrained in arriving
at the conclusion I have reached in this case.

[
53
]

I find the comments of Finlayson J.A. at para. 25
of
Normart Management
more useful in providing guidance for the
present situation:

This bare
allegation of a conspiracy involving the directing minds of the respondent
corporations is an impermissible legal proposition.  Additionally, it is very
difficult to fit it into either of the two categories referred to in
Canada

Cement
LaFarge
,
supra
.  There is no allegation of a predominant purpose
to injure under (1) or of unlawful acts under (2).  The acts of the individual
respondents are not unlawful
per se
. They are not parties to the
contract in issue and have no personal obligation to the appellant or to its
principal Yakubowicz, either contractual or fiduciary.  Simply reciting a
series of events and stating that they were intended to injure the appellant is
hardly sufficient to establish a conspiracy at law particularly where the same
facts have already been pleaded in support of an action for breach of contract.
The basis in law of a stand-alone conspiracy is simply not established.

[
54
]

Similarly, in the present case, there is no
allegation of a predominant purpose to injure and none of Mr. Punja’s actions
are unlawful
per se
.  To paraphrase Finlayson J.A.’s remarks in
Normart
Management
, simply reciting a series of events and saying that one
defendant who had not committed a wrongful act”, agreed with two others who had
allegedly committed wrongful acts is hardly sufficient to establish a
conspiracy at law against the first defendant.  Accordingly, there is no basis
for a stand-alone conspiracy claim against Mr. Punja in the circumstances set
out in the amended statement of claim.

Conspiracy
Claim Against Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja

[
55
]

I accept the Bank’s position that the amended
statement of claim does allege actual damage to the Bank from the conspiracy to
wrongfully split the commissions.  The more pressing issue with regard to these
conspiracy claims is whether they merge in the other allegations of breach of
contract and fiduciary duty.  The defendants rely on the statement of the
merger principle in
Hovsepian v. Westfair Foods Ltd.
,
2001 ABQB
700
, [2001] 10 W.W.R. 504 at paras.
116-17
:

In
Ward v. Lewis
,
[1955] 1 All E.R.
55 (Eng. C.A.)
, the court held that a conspiracy allegation failed, so the
plaintiff was denied leave to amend his statement of claim. Lord Denning stated
at 56:

It is important
to remember that when a tort has been committed by two or more persons an
allegation of a prior conspiracy to commit the tort adds nothing. The prior
agreement merges in the tort....When the court sees attempts [to get an added
advantage], it will discourage them by striking out the allegation of
conspiracy on the simple ground that the conspiracy adds nothing when the tort
has in fact been committed.

Normart
Management Ltd.
, supra at 102 (Ont. C.A.), relied
on the merger principle in striking out conspiracy allegations, as it was clear
that the plaintiff was attempting to convert its breach of contract and breach
of fiduciary action into a conspiracy action against a broader range of parties
by alleging the same factual basis and damages.

[
56
]

In
Napoleone
, Pitfield J. relied
on
Hovespian
in deciding that the merger principle prevented the
plaintiff from pursuing a conspiracy claim against all of the defendants.

[
57
]

I find that the merger principle applies in
these circumstances.  The allegation of conspiracy adds nothing to the
allegations against Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja.  The breaches of contract and
fiduciary duties have, allegedly, been committed.  This is not a case like
Hunt

where the conspiracy claim was permitted to stand because the wrongful acts
alleged in the conspiracy claim were different from the wrongful acts that were
alleged to be the basis of the tort.  Here, the wrongful acts, breach of
contract and breach of fiduciary duty, are the same as those that give rise to
the conspiracy allegation.  Accordingly, it is plain and obvious that the
statement of claim does not disclose a reasonable cause of action.

The only question that remains is whether the conspiracy claims
should be struck with leave to amend.  I am not persuaded that this is an
appropriate case to permit an amendment.  The Bank has now tried twice with two
very different sets of allegations and has failed to disclose a reasonable
claim in conspiracy.  The conspiracy claims are dismissed without leave to
amend.
